articles.title: Why modern love has to start with a self-audit
articles.excerpt: Most people evaluating a relationship are running the assessment on the wrong person. Here is what happens when you turn the instrument around.
body: Almost everyone who comes to me with a relationship problem arrives holding a file on somebody else. They have dates. They have quotes. They have a pattern of behaviour documented across months, sometimes years. What they almost never have is a file on themselves.

This is not dishonesty. It is the ordinary architecture of attention: we experience our own behaviour as reasonable responses to circumstance, and other people's behaviour as character. So the audit gets run on the partner, and the audit comes back conclusive, and nothing changes.
## The question that reframes it
In risk assessment we never ask whether a system is fine. Fine is not a measurable state. We ask a different question: where is this exposed, and what happens at the moment that point fails?

Turn that on yourself and it stops being an exercise in self-criticism. You are not asking whether you are a good person. You are asking which parts of you have never been tested, and what will happen the first time they are.
> You do not find the right person. You become one. This is the hardest thing I say to singles, and the truest.
## What a self-audit actually examines
- Self-knowledge — can you name a trigger before it fires, or only afterwards?
- Emotional regulation — when you are hurt, can you stay in the conversation?
- Inherited patterns — what did the home you grew up in teach you about love, and what have you decided not to repeat?
- Capacity — does your life currently have room in it for another person's needs?
- Repair — do you know how to apologise without conditions, excuses, or the word 'but'?
Notice that none of those are about your partner. That is the point. Every one of them is something you carry into the next relationship regardless of who it is with.
## The uncomfortable arithmetic

If you have had three relationships end for broadly the same reason, the common factor is not bad luck and it is not a run of unsuitable people. This is an uncomfortable thing to notice, and it is the single most useful realisation available to anyone reading this.
It is also good news, structurally. You cannot change a partner. You have considerable authority over yourself.

The self-audit takes about ten minutes. It will not diagnose you and it will not tell you whether to leave anyone. It will show you, in five dimensions, where you are strong and where you are exposed — which is the only place any real work can start.

articles.title: The five exposure points in every marriage
articles.excerpt: Catastrophes are almost never sudden. They are the visible moment of a failure that has been accumulating quietly, somewhere nobody was looking.
body: In the energy sector I spent years looking at systems and answering one question honestly: where is this exposed, and what happens when that point fails? The answer was never that a system failed suddenly. It failed slowly, in a place nobody had been asked to inspect, and then it failed visibly on a Tuesday.
Marriages behave the same way. In more than two decades of practice I have watched the same five exposure points account for the overwhelming majority of what arrives in my room.
## 1. Unaudited individuals

Two people who have never examined their own histories will reliably re-enact them on each other. Neither is acting in bad faith. They are each running software written in a house they no longer live in.
## 2. No repair protocol

Every couple ruptures. The question is not whether you fight but whether you have a reliable, practised way back. Couples with no repair protocol do not fight less — they simply let the silence do the work, and silence compounds.
> Rupture is normal. Unrepaired rupture is fatal.
## 3. Undeclared third parties

A third party is not always an affair. It is a mother who is consulted before the spouse. A friend who hears the complaint first. A previous relationship that still sets the standard. Where the boundary sits, and who defends it, decides whether the marriage has two members or five.
## 4. Silent withdrawal

This is the most dangerous of the five because it presents as peace. One partner stops raising things, having decided they are not worth the cost. The house goes quiet. Both people describe the marriage as 'fine' right up until one of them leaves.
## 5. No scheduled review

Businesses review. Buildings are inspected. Bodies get check-ups. Marriages are expected to run for fifty years on hope and good intentions, with no scheduled point at which anyone asks how it is actually doing.
## What to do with this

You cannot fix an exposure point you have not named. The Relational Risk Assessment walks through all five in about twelve minutes and returns a written picture of where your relationship is solid and where it is thin.
It is not a verdict. It is an inspection — and inspections are cheapest before the failure, not after.

articles.title: I assessed risk in the energy sector. Here's what it taught me about marriage.
articles.excerpt: The discipline transferred almost perfectly. So did the thing nobody wants to hear about how failures actually happen.
body: I did not begin in psychology. My early career was in the energy sector, in security and risk assessment, and my job was to look at a system and tell the truth about it.
The discipline is unglamorous. You do not look for what is working. You look for the single point whose failure takes everything else with it, and you ask what happens on the day it goes.
## The transfer

What I started noticing was that capable, senior, accomplished people — people who would never sign off on an unassessed system at work — went home to relationships they had no framework for at all. No assessment. No maintenance schedule. No repair protocol. Just hope, and the assumption that love would cover what nobody had ever been taught to build.
> Nobody would run a refinery on good intentions. A great many people run a marriage that way.
## Three things risk work teaches you
- Failures are almost never sudden. They are visible suddenly. That is a different claim.
- The dangerous problem is the unmonitored one, not the loud one. A loud problem is already being managed.
- Inspection is not pessimism. Refusing to inspect is not optimism — it is a decision to be surprised later.
## What it does not transfer to
People are not systems, and I want to be careful here. You cannot engineer a spouse, and the language of risk becomes cruel the moment it is used to make a person into a liability.

What transfers is the discipline of honest attention: the willingness to look directly at the part you have been avoiding, name it accurately, and act while it is still small. That is all an assessment is. The rest of the work is human, and slow, and done together.

articles.title: The quiet exit: how marriages actually end
articles.excerpt: Long before anyone leaves the house, somebody leaves the conversation. Here is what that looks like from the inside.
body: Most people imagine a marriage ends in a scene. In my experience it ends in a series of small, reasonable decisions not to bother.

Somebody raises something and it goes badly. They raise it again a month later and it goes badly again. The third time, they weigh the cost, decide the subject is not worth the evening it will consume, and let it go. Nothing dramatic has happened. A door has quietly closed.
## Why it presents as peace

The house gets calmer. The arguments stop. From the outside — and often from one partner's inside — this reads as things settling down. It is why the person who eventually leaves is so frequently described as having left 'out of nowhere'. It was not nowhere. It was a series of closed doors nobody counted.
> When a marriage gets quiet, the useful question is not 'are we fighting less?' It is 'what have we stopped talking about?'
## The inventory
Sit down separately and write the list of subjects you have stopped raising. Money. Sex. Their mother. The way they speak to you in front of other people. Your own disappointment. Then compare lists.
Couples find this exercise unpleasant and clarifying in roughly equal measure. The lists are almost never the same length, and that asymmetry is usually the most important information in the room.
## If you are the one who has gone quiet

You are not being difficult by wanting to be heard, and you are not obliged to keep spending yourself on conversations that reliably cost more than they return. But withdrawal is a strategy with a terminal cost, and it is worth knowing that you are paying it.
## If you are the one who has not noticed

The absence of complaint is not evidence of contentment. Ask directly, and then — this is the part that decides everything — receive the answer without defending yourself. One conversation held properly can reopen a door that has been shut for years.

articles.title: In-laws: where the boundary goes, and who defends it
articles.excerpt: In our context, marriage joins families as well as people. That is a strength and it is an exposure point. Both things are true.
body: I want to say something carefully, because it is easy to get wrong in both directions.

In our culture, a marriage joins two families. That is not a defect to be corrected with imported advice about cutting people off. Extended family is a genuine source of support, continuity, and care, and couples who sever it often find they have solved one problem by creating three.
It is also, reliably, one of the five places a marriage becomes exposed.
## The distinction that matters
The question is almost never whether family is involved. It is whether the couple is the decision-making unit, and whether both partners know it.
> Influence is welcome. Authority is not transferable. The moment a third party has authority over a decision that belongs to the two of you, you no longer have a marriage of two people.
## Who defends the boundary
Here is the rule I hold to, and I hold to it firmly: each partner is responsible for their own family of origin.

A wife should not be negotiating with her husband's mother about her husband's mother's expectations. He should. A husband should not be the one managing his wife's siblings. She should. When this is reversed — when each person is left to defend themselves against the other's family — the marriage acquires a permanent adversarial seam.
This is not about disrespect. It is entirely possible to be warm, deferential, and generous to your parents while making it unmistakable that your household's decisions are made in your household.
## The three conversations to have before it is tested
- Money. What is given, to whom, how much, and who decides. Vague generosity becomes specific resentment.
- Access. Visits, duration, notice. A door that is always open belongs to everyone.
- Information. What is discussed with family before it is discussed with each other — and, more importantly, what is not.
Have these while things are calm. Boundaries negotiated during a crisis are experienced as attacks; boundaries agreed in peacetime are experienced as structure.

articles.title: What to do when your partner won't come to counselling
articles.excerpt: Starting alone works far more often than people expect. Here is why, and what it does and does not achieve.
body: This is the single most common message I receive: some version of 'I want to do this and he won't come', or 'she thinks it means we've failed'.
The short answer is: start anyway.
## Why it works more often than you'd think

A relationship is a system, and systems respond to a changed input. When one person becomes markedly better at regulating themselves, at raising things early, at apologising cleanly and not retaliating, the pattern between the two of you cannot continue in exactly its old form. It has lost a participant.

I am not promising this converts a reluctant partner. Sometimes it does — a surprising number of people book their own first session after watching someone else change for three months. But that is a possible side effect, not the goal.
> Do not go to therapy as a manoeuvre to change someone else. Go because you would rather be well than be right.
## What individual work will do
- Show you your own contribution with enough precision to act on it
- Give you a repair protocol you can run from your side
- Separate what is genuinely happening from what your history is telling you is happening
- Get you clear enough to make a decision you can live with
## What it will not do

It will not diagnose your partner in absentia. I will not accept a description of someone who is not in the room and treat it as fact — not because I doubt you, but because it is not honest practice and it would not serve you.
And it will not tell you whether to stay. That decision is yours, and my job is to make sure that when you make it, you make it with clear eyes rather than out of exhaustion.
## On the reluctance itself

Most refusal is not indifference. It is fear of being blamed for an hour with a stranger, and it is often worth saying plainly: counselling is not court. I am not here to decide who is right. If someone leaves my room feeling they won, I have failed at my job.
That sentence has brought more reluctant partners through my door than any argument I know.

articles.title: Is counselling against your faith? A direct answer.
articles.excerpt: It is a fair question, asked sincerely and often. It deserves something better than a defensive answer.
body: People ask me this quietly, usually near the end of a first conversation, and often with some embarrassment. There is nothing embarrassing about it. It is a serious question about how you have been taught to seek help, and it deserves a direct answer rather than a defensive one.
## The short answer
No. Seeking skilled help is not a failure of faith, and I have never met a serious faith tradition that teaches otherwise when the subject is a broken leg rather than a broken marriage.
> Nobody prays over a fracture and declines the cast. The theology does not change because the injury is invisible.
## Where the worry usually comes from
In my experience the concern is rarely about counselling itself. It is about three specific fears, and each one is answerable.
- That a therapist will tell you to leave. I will not. I do not make that decision for anyone; I help people get clear enough to make it themselves and live with it.
- That your beliefs will be treated as the problem. They will not. Your faith is part of your context and, very often, part of your resources. I work with it, not against it.
- That it replaces spiritual counsel. It does not. Pastoral care and clinical work do different jobs, and the people who do best usually have both.
## What I actually do
I am a psychotherapist. I work with patterns, history, capacity, regulation and repair. I do not adjudicate doctrine, and I will not pretend to a spiritual authority I do not have.

If your faith community is a source of strength for you, bring it. If it is a source of pressure — and for some people, particularly women being counselled to endure things they should not endure, it is — then that is worth examining honestly too, and you will not be judged for saying so out loud.

articles.title: Twenty-five years married: nine things I'd tell my younger self
articles.excerpt: Not advice from a podium. Notes from someone who has been doing this a long time and got a number of things wrong first.
body: I have been married for twenty-five years and I have been a therapist for a good deal of that. Those two facts do not make me an authority on your marriage. They do mean I have made most of the ordinary mistakes personally before I ever saw them professionally.
Here is what I would tell the woman who got married at the start of it.
## One
You will spend the first years trying to be understood and the later years learning to understand. The second is more work and it is the one that actually changes the temperature of a house.
## Two
Being right is nearly worthless. I say this to couples constantly and I had to learn it at home first. There is no prize, and the cost of collecting it is always paid by the relationship.
## Three
Learn to apologise properly. No conditions, no explanation of why you were provoked, and no 'but'. The word 'but' deletes everything in the sentence before it.
> Repair is a skill, not a temperament. Skills can be taught, practised, and improved at any age.
## Four
Your parents are in your marriage whether you invited them or not. The only question is whether you have noticed and decided which parts stay.
## Five
Silence is not peace. When it got quiet, I used to feel relieved. I now know that a quiet house is a house to ask questions in.
## Six
Money conversations are never about money. They are about safety, fairness, and who is allowed to want things.
## Seven

Do the maintenance. Once a year, sit down and actually review it — not logistics, not the children, the marriage. Every couple I know who does this finds something small. Every couple who doesn't finds something large, later.
## Eight
You cannot make someone else do the work. You can do yours and let the system respond. It often does.
## Nine
The marriage will only ever be as healthy as the two people in it. This is the whole of my practice in one line, and I did not learn it in a lecture theatre.
